To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative risk parameter estimates from the stratified analysis are unbiased and have the highest efficiency of the three analyses, the analytic random effects analysis is unbiased and has the second highest efficiency, and the aggregate random effects analysis has the lowest efficiency.

(1) the analytic random effects estimator is the most precise, unbiased, and robust estimator for relative rate parameters in this model, and (2) the aggregate random effects estimator is biased when there is confounding or covariate measurement error, and its bias is a function of the degree of confounding or covariates measurement error.

1) aggregate random effects analysis is the most efficient and unbiased analysis; 2) stratified analysis is more efficient than analytic random effects analysis, but is biased in the presence of confounding; and 3) analytic random effects analysis is unbiased in the presence of covariate dispersion and confounding, but is less efficient than the other two analyses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reliability and precision (efficiency) of within- and among-population estimates of relative rate (hazard) parameters, which are of fundamental importance in the analysis of survival data.
the reliability of relative risk estimates in epidemiologic studies, and the effect of confounding, covariate dispersion, and covariate error on these estimates.
the development and evaluation of a method of analysis for multigroup studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the aggregate-level analyses are generally more efficient than the stratified analyses, and that the analytic random effects analyses are generally more precise than the aggregate random effects analyses, but that the stratified analyses provide a more precise estimate of the relative rate parameters than the analytic random effects analysis.

the aggregate random effects approach is preferred for estimating the relative rate of a covariate, when the covariate is measured with error, the covariate is not strongly confounded with the outcome and there is no strong correlation between the covariate and error term.
, for a multigroup relative rate analysis of a continuous outcome variable, the aggregate-level analysis provides the most reliable and precise estimates of relative rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aggregate level analysis is the most efficient method of estimation.
, in general, aggregate-level analyses provide more precise estimates of the relative rate parameters.
aggregate-level analysis is a good alternative to individual-level analysis when covariate dispersion is large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
aggregate level analyses are generally more efficient and less prone to confounding than individual level analyses.
aggregate-level estimates can be very reliable, but that the reliability is highly dependent on the covariate dispersion, the confounding structure, and the amount of measurement error.
, for a given analysis method, there is a tradeoff between precision and bias.
